english: Plaster / lime / mortar / sand / cement / concrete
keywords: Plaster / lime / mortar / sand / cement / concrete tēctōrium, tēctōriī n. Ancient words Modern technical senses tēctōrium, tēctōriī n. — plaster / plaster coating; мазилка . Traupman p. 168; Palladius discusses applying and levelling it. calx, calcis f. — lime; вар . Do not silently equate lime with modern cement; Traupman’s English cement gloss is too broad for buying modern building materials. harēna, harēnae f. — sand; пясък . harēnātum, harēnātī n. — lime-and-sand mortar; варо-пясъчен разтвор . Traupman p. 168, and also classical: Cato, Agr. 18.7 dē glāreā et calce harēnātō ; Vitruvius 7.3.5; Pliny, NH 36.176 (Lewis & Short). Mortar is строителен разтвор; хоросан commonly means lime-based mortar. lithocolla, lithocollae f. — cement; цимент . Recorded for modern cemento in the Vatican’s public abridgement. The unmarked modern stem vowels are not claimed to have independently established quantities. opus caementīcium, operis caementīciī n. — concrete; бетон . The modern name for Roman concrete, built on Vitruvius’s caementīcius , “of rubble stones” ( in caementīciīs autem strūctūrīs , 2.4.1; parietibus caementīciīs , 2.8.17); used here for modern concrete too. Traupman p. 168 has concrētum , which is not used: classical concrētus means “thickened, congealed”. Classical mortar and rubble terms: māteria, māteriae f. — in Vitruvius also the mixed mortar (2.5.1; 2.8.2); caementa, caementōrum n. pl. — rough quarry stones / rubble laid in mortar; ломен камък ; rūdus, rūderis n. — broken stone mixed with lime for floors; statūmen n. — the bottom bedding layer of a floor (Vitruvius 7.1.1). Tēctōrium parietī indūcunt. — They are applying plaster to the wall. Полагат мазилка върху стената.

keywords: Insulation / insulation board / panel īnsulātiō, īnsulātiōnis f. īnsulātiō, īnsulātiōnis f. — insulation; изолация . Morgan–Owens records insulatio, citing Helfer; the brief entry does not specify a complete thermal-insulation system. īnsulātiō thermica — thermal insulation; топлоизолация . Our explicit thermal qualifier, not an independently verified complete entry. tabula ad calōrem retinendum — insulation board, described as a board for retaining heat; топлоизолационна плоча . Our functional description. For an individual panel, tabula, tabulae f. is a useful broad noun; the precise material should be specified separately. tabula spūmea; tabulae spūmeae f. — EPS insulation board (expanded polystyrene); EPS плоча / стиропор . Our working formation, not an attested term, built on classical spūmeus, spūmea, spūmeum “foamy” (Vergil, Ovid, Pliny). Gloss: tabula levissima ex māteriā artificiōsā spūmeā facta, quae parietibus forīs affīgitur, ut domus hieme calōrem retineat et aestāte frīgus. The common boards on site are black, graphite EPS ( графитен EPS / графитен стиропор ), not white. mūnīmentum adversus frīgus — protection against the cold; parietēs adversus frīgus mūnīre — insulate the walls. Our functional descriptions, preferable in narration because īnsulātiō collides with īnsula . Classical model for the function: Columella 9.7.4 quod tegumen cum frīgora et pluviās tum et aestūs arcet . Nōlī hanc tabulam perforāre. — Don’t make holes in this board. Не пробивай тази плоча.

latin: terra, terrae f.; sordēs, sordium f. pl.
keywords: Dirt / soil / grime terra, terrae f.; sordēs, sordium f. pl. terra, terrae f. — dirt as earth or soil; the ordinary material dug out of a trench. sordēs, sordium f. pl. — dirt as grime or filth. A singular also exists; the plural is the useful everyday form given here. Terram hūc fer. — Bring the dirt here. Sordēs ē manibus terge. — Wipe the dirt off your hands. The English noun covers both the building material and unwanted dirt on a surface; Latin makes that distinction without requiring different kinds of soil. latin: tumulus, tumulī m.; acervus, acervī m.
keywords: Mound / pile (noun) / pile up (verb) tumulus, tumulī m.; acervus, acervī m. tumulus, tumulī m. — raised heap of earth, mound or small hill. The noun also has a burial-mound sense, prominent in poetry (Vergil, Ecl. 5.42 tumulum facite ), but is not restricted to graves; a hillock is larger than a child’s heap. cumulus, cumulī m. — heap; our recommendation for a child’s heap of sand, gravel or dirt. Vergil, G. 1.105 cumulōsque … harēnae ; Ovid, Met. 14.137 pulveris … cumulum . acervus, acervī m. — heap or pile. acervus terrae — pile of dirt; acervus lapidum — pile of stones. cumulō, cumulāre, cumulāvī, cumulātum — heap / pile up; transitive. Lewis & Short gives material objects including sand, snow and logs, and marks the physical sense as mostly post-Augustan. coacervō, coacervāre, coacervāvī, coacervātum — heap together. Terram hīc cumulā. — Pile the dirt here. Lapidēs in acervum congere. — Heap the stones into a pile. congerō, congerere, congessī, congestum — bring or heap together. congestus, congestūs m. — a heaping up, a heap; Seneca, Const. 12.2 has children who in lītoribus harēnae congestū simulācra domuum excitant . This is “pile” meaning a heap, not a foundation pile driven into the ground. Lapidēs in acervum congere. — Heap the stones into a pile. congerō, congerere, congessī, congestum — bring or heap together. congestus, congestūs m. — a heaping up, a heap; Seneca, Const. 12.2 has children who in lītoribus harēnae congestū simulācra domuum excitant.
This is “pile” meaning a heap, not a foundation pile driven into the ground.

keywords: Scaffold / scaffolding / framework māchina, māchinae f. māchina, māchinae f. — scaffold / scaffolding for building, the Roman word. Digest 13.6.5.7 (Ulpian): a plasterer lent out falls dē māchinā ; the risk differs if he was lent to work dē plānō , on the ground, or if the scaffold was minus dīligenter … ligāta or failed through fūnium perticārumque vetustāte . Vitruvius 7.2.2 māchinīs comparātīs (scaffolds set up for vaulting rooms); Vitruvius 10.1.1 scānsōriae māchinae , built tignīs statūtīs et trānsversāriīs conligātīs . Lewis & Short I.B.3 also cites Pliny 19.2.8 §30 (NH 19.30), but there māchinīs aedificātiōnum means building machinery such as hoists, which is weak evidence for scaffolding. The noun is broader than modern English “machine.” Morgan–Owens also lists it under scaffolding. arrēctāria, arrēctāriōrum n. pl.; trānsversāria, trānsversāriōrum n. pl. — uprights and crosspieces, Vitruvius’s names for the members; see the scaffold-members entry . compāgēs, compāgis f. — joining, joint, framework (Lewis & Short: “a joining together, connection, joint, structure,” used of the body and the state). Classically it never names a builder’s scaffold; the scaffolding sense is modern lexicographic (Morgan–Owens). Useful as a gloss word, not as the narrative noun. māchina ex fistulīs ferreīs — scaffolding made of iron tubes; our descriptive phrase for the modern construction-site object. Operārius in māchinā stat. — The worker is standing on the scaffold. Māchinam juxtā domum cōnstruunt. — They are assembling the scaffolding beside the house. Dē plānō lūde, nōn in māchinā. — Play on the ground, not on the scaffold; after the Digest’s dē plānō . These sentences are composed. pēgma, pēgmatis n. is another ancient framework/machinery noun, especially for theatrical stage machinery and board fixtures. Its ancient examples do not by themselves establish the modern tube-and-clamp construction sense; māchina has the clearer explicit builder’s-scaffold entry. english: Scaffold pole / upright / crossbar / diagonal brace
latin: arrēctārium, arrēctāriī n.; trānsversārium, trānsversāriī n.
keywords: Scaffold pole / upright / crossbar / diagonal brace arrēctārium, arrēctāriī n.; trānsversārium, trānsversāriī n. arrēctārium, arrēctāriī n. , usually plural arrēctāria — upright, standard. Vitruvius 2.8.20 arrēctāriōrum et trānsversāriōrum dispositiōne and 7.3.11 in arrēctāriīs et trānsversāriīs , of the posts of timber-framed walls; 10.13.4 of the uprights of siege towers. Lewis & Short: “the upright posts of a wall.” Applied here to the steel standards of a tube scaffold. trānsversārium, trānsversāriī n. — crosspiece; ledger / transom. Vitruvius 10.1.1 tignīs statūtīs et trānsversāriīs conligātīs ; 2.8.20; Caesar, BC 2.15 has tigna trānsversāria (Lewis & Short). One noun serves both horizontal functions; Latin does not distinguish ledger and transom. pertica, perticae f. — pole; the Digest’s word for the poles of a lashed Roman scaffold (13.6.5.7 fūnium perticārumque vetustāte ). fistula, fistulae f.; fistula ferrea; tubus ferreus — tube; iron tube. Material glosses for the hollow steel member, not member names; classically a fistula is first a (lead) water pipe, and tubus a pipe. For a wooden pole or beam, asser, asseris m. is ancient; the shape and material determine which noun fits. fistula ad perpendiculum posita — upright / vertical tube, literally a tube placed plumb; our description; the classical member name is arrēctārium . Ancient ad perpendiculum means vertically / perpendicularly. ferrum trānsversum; ferrī trānsversī n. — crossbar / horizontal metal bar. Morgan–Owens and Traupman record it in gymnastics; applying it to this scaffold bar is our contextual extension. fistula trānsversa specifies a hollow cross-tube. The classical member name is trānsversārium . fulcīmentum, fulcīmentī n. — prop, stay or support; an ancient post-classical noun. fulcīmentum oblīquum — diagonal brace, our functional description. oblīquus, oblīqua, oblīquum means slanting / diagonal. Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit. — Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. Our full composed version of the site example. english: Scaffold platform / deck / plank / guardrails / base plate / ladder
latin: tabulātum, tabulātī n.; tabula, tabulae f.
keywords: Scaffold platform / deck / plank / guardrails / base plate / ladder tabulātum, tabulātī n.; tabula, tabulae f. tabulātum, tabulātī n. — planked flooring, floor or platform; applied here to the scaffold’s working deck. The floor/storey sense also appears in the existing house-layout entry; Vitruvius 10.13.4 has a siege tower tabulātōrum decem . Vergil, A. 9.530 turris erat vastō suspectū et pontibus altīs : pontēs , high gangways, a poetic model for walk-boards. tabula, tabulae f. — plank / board; an individual wooden plank of the deck. A metal deck is a modern application of the platform vocabulary, not evidence that ancient platforms used the same fittings. repāgula, repāgulōrum n. pl. — bars / barriers, ancient especially for door bars; our functional extension to guardrails. ferrum trānsversum ad marginem tabulātī positum describes one metal rail placed at the edge of the deck. Neither is asserted to be a standardized modern scaffold-component term. Closer ancient words for a parapet: pluteus, pluteī m. — breastwork, parapet on towers (Caesar, BG 7.41, per Lewis & Short); lōrīca, lōrīcae f. — breastwork, parapet (Caesar, per Lewis & Short). lāmina, lāminae f. — plate / sheet. lāmina sub fistulā posita — base plate under a scaffold tube; our description, not a verified technical compound. scālae, scālārum f. pl. — ladder / stairs; gradus, gradūs m. — step or ladder rung. See the existing stairs / ladder entry . Operārius super tabulātum ambulat. — The worker is walking on the platform. This is vocabulary for describing the scene, not an assembly specification. english: Scaffold joint / coupler / assemble / brace / dismantle
keywords: Scaffold joint / coupler / assemble / brace / dismantle jūnctūra, jūnctūrae f.; cōnstruō, cōnstruere jūnctūra, jūnctūrae f. — joining / joint / connection; the ancient general noun is applied here to the joint between scaffold members. vinculum, vinculī n. — fastening / bond / tie. vinculum quō duae fistulae conjunguntur — a fastening by which two tubes are joined; our descriptive “coupler / clamp.” It describes the function rather than claiming a specific modern coupler design had an ancient name. ligō, ligāre, ligāvī, ligātum — tie, lash; the Digest’s verb for a Roman scaffold (13.6.5.7 māchinae … nōn ab ipsō ligātae ). retinācula, retināculōrum n. pl. — ropes, stays, ties (Cato, Vergil, Vitruvius, per Lewis & Short); applied here to the ties anchoring the scaffold to the wall. cōnstruō, cōnstruere, cōnstrūxī, cōnstrūctum — construct / build; here assemble. ērigō, ērigere — raise / erect. conjungō, conjungere — connect / join together. firmō, firmāre — secure / make firm; fulciō, fulcīre — prop up / brace / support. dissolvō, dissolvere, dissolvī, dissolūtum — take apart / dismantle; the verb has ancient use for taking apart a bridge. Fistulās inter sē conjungunt. — They are connecting the tubes together. Māchinam fulcīmentīs firmant. — They are securing the scaffold with braces. Māchinam dissolvunt. — They are dismantling the scaffold. The verbs are ancient; the full modern-scaffold applications and sample sentences are ours. The ancient member names ( arrēctāria , trānsversāria ) are attested; only the steel coupler and adjustable base jack are modern, and no exact Latin names for them have been verified in the named sources.
